title: Chemistry's Shorthand, Decoded
question: How do you read a chemical equation and tell if it is right?
hook: One line of symbols can say what goes in, what comes out, and what energy is added.
idea: An equation puts reactants on the left and products on the right, and it is balanced when every element has the same atom count on both sides.

beats.prompt: You count atoms in a draft equation: 3 oxygen atoms on the left, 2 on the right. What should you conclude?

choices.label: Oxygen was destroyed in the reaction
choices.feedback: No nuclear reactions take place in a chemical reaction, so the elements pass through unchanged and nothing is destroyed.

choices.label: It is fine as long as the arrow points toward the products
choices.feedback: The arrow shows direction, but a balanced equation needs the same number of atoms of each element on both sides.

choices.label: It is not balanced, so the coefficients need adjusting

beats.explain: Each side must show the same number of atoms of an element, and an equation is balanced by assigning suitable coefficients.

beats.prompt: Match each piece of notation to what it tells you.
pairs: How many entities of a substance take part
beats.explain: Coefficients count entities, plus signs separate substances, and Δ and hν show the form of added energy.

beats.prompt: Sort each item by where it is written.
beats.explain: Energy and medium symbols go on the arrow, while formulas and their coefficients are written in the reactant and product sides.

beats.prompt: One step in this reasoning is wrong. Which?
steps: Elements pass through a chemical reaction unchanged.
So each side of the equation must show the same number of atoms of each element.
An equation that meets this is said to be balanced.
So to balance an equation, you change the small numbers inside each formula.
beats.explain: A chemical equation is balanced by assigning suitable values to the stoichiometric coefficients.
